source_facts: Ledgerwake is a synthetic event-ledger service. A read window is opened with POST /v1/windows and a stream name. Opening a window fixes an upper committed offset; events committed afterward are outside that window. The response supplies window_id, first_cursor, and expires_at. A window expires exactly 20 minutes after creation, regardless of read activity. A page is fetched with GET /v1/windows/{window_id}/pages?cursor={cursor}. Page size is fixed at 200 events except that the final page may be shorter. Within a window, events are returned in ascending offset order. Each page has events and next_cursor. A null next_cursor means the window is exhausted. The client must follow next_cursor rather than derive a cursor from event IDs or page length. Cursors are opaque and are scoped to the window that issued them. Reusing the same cursor before expiration returns the same event sequence. Page delivery is at least once because clients can repeat requests. Ledgerwake event_id is stable across windows and is the deduplication key. Clients should atomically persist their downstream effects and next_cursor after processing a page. If this is not possible, downstream writes must be idempotent by event_id. An expired window request returns HTTP 410. Recovery from expiration opens a new window from the last durably committed offset, inclusively, so the boundary event can be delivered again. This offset is a recovery checkpoint, not a decoded cursor. An empty stream produces an empty events array with null next_cursor. Opening another window is the way to read events committed after the original upper offset. Window reads do not acknowledge, remove, or change retention of source events. Consumers maintain their own checkpoints. The service does not extend expiration when pages are fetched or retried. No ingestion programming language or storage transaction mechanism is prescribed.

# Understanding Ledgerwake read windows

Ledgerwake exposes event-ledger reads as bounded windows. This model lets an ingestion client work through a stable portion of a stream while producers continue committing new events. The reader maintains its own progress; fetching a page does not acknowledge an event, remove it, or change its retention in the source ledger. This guide describes the state a resumable client needs to retain.

## Values returned by the service

Open a window with POST /v1/windows and the stream name. The response includes window_id, first_cursor, and expires_at. Fetch a page with GET /v1/windows/{window_id}/pages?cursor={cursor}. Each page contains events and next_cursor. Page size is fixed at 200 events, except that the final page can be shorter. An empty stream produces an empty events array and a null next_cursor.

The event_id is stable across windows and is the key for deduplicating downstream writes. Window reads provide at-least-once page delivery because a client may repeat a request. The source ledger and the downstream destination therefore have separate notions of progress: receiving a response does not itself prove that the destination has committed its effects.

## Window expiration

A window expires exactly 20 minutes after creation. Reading pages or retrying them does not extend that deadline. A request against an expired window returns HTTP 410. Treat expires_at as the boundary for this particular window, rather than as an inactivity timer that successful traffic will refresh.

For recovery after expiration, open a new window from the last durably committed offset. That start offset is inclusive, so the boundary event can be delivered again. The offset is a recovery checkpoint maintained by the consumer; it is not a value obtained by decoding a cursor.

## The fixed boundary

Opening a window fixes its upper committed offset. Events committed after that point are outside the window, even if the client has not yet fetched its first page. Within a window, events are returned in ascending offset order. To consume events committed after the upper boundary, open another window after completing the current one.

A null next_cursor means the current window is exhausted. Follow the returned next_cursor to advance; do not derive a cursor from event IDs or from the length of the events array. A short final page is compatible with the page-size limit, but the explicit null value is the completion signal a client should use.

## Committing downstream work

After processing a page, atomically persist its downstream effects and next_cursor. This keeps the saved continuation position aligned with the work the destination has actually accepted. If those writes cannot share a transaction, make downstream writes idempotent by event_id. The service does not prescribe a programming language or a particular storage transaction mechanism for implementing that guarantee.

## Cursor identity

Cursors are opaque and belong to the window that issued them. A cursor from one window cannot serve as the continuation position for another. Reusing the same cursor before expiration returns the same event sequence, which permits a client to retry a page whose processing outcome is uncertain. That repeatability is local to the active window; it does not turn the cursor into a permanent recovery checkpoint.

requirements.description: Preserve POST /v1/windows as the operation that opens a window.
State that opening a window fixes its upper committed offset.
State that events committed after the fixed upper offset are outside the window.
Preserve the fixed page size of 200 events except for a potentially shorter final page.
State that null next_cursor signals window exhaustion.
Require following the returned next_cursor to advance.
State that a cursor is scoped to its issuing window.
State that reusing a cursor before expiration returns the same event sequence.
Preserve expiration at 20 minutes after creation regardless of read activity.
Preserve HTTP 410 as the expired-window response.
State that expiration recovery begins inclusively at the last durably committed offset.
Identify event_id as the cross-window deduplication key.
Require atomic persistence of downstream effects with next_cursor when a shared transaction is available.
Require idempotent downstream writes by event_id when atomic persistence is unavailable.
State that reading a window does not remove source events.

issues.description: The fixed-boundary model is explained only after response fields, delivery guarantees, expiration, and recovery, so readers must reinterpret those earlier details after learning what a window actually bounds.
issues.acceptable_resolution: Establish the window boundary before dependent details, or provide an early concise model with clear links to its elaboration. A lifecycle narrative, concept-first explanation, or another coherent progression is acceptable.

issues.description: Continuation, cursor repeatability, downstream commit behavior, and inclusive expiration recovery are distributed across four separated sections without navigation that explains their relationship.
issues.acceptable_resolution: Make the relationships among normal continuation, retry, durable checkpoints, and expiration recovery easy to follow through regrouping, a connecting explanation, or precise cross-references. Preserve the distinction between a cursor and a recovery offset.
